content: Insulin injections are prescribed to manage blood sugar levels in individuals with type 1 diabetes, where the body does not produce insulin, and in those with type 2 diabetes, where the body either does not produce enough insulin or cannot use it effectively. Insulin is used when oral medications alone are insufficient to control blood sugar. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones and replaces the insulin that the body would normally produce. Insulin works by facilitating the movement of sugar from the bloodstream into body tissues, where it is used for energy. All types of insulin function in this way, but they differ in how quickly they start working and how long they continue to control blood sugar. Insulin is available as a solution (a liquid) or a suspension (a liquid with particles that settle when standing) and is injected subcutaneously (under the skin). It is typically administered multiple times a day, and more than one type of insulin may be required. Your doctor will specify the type(s) of insulin, the dosage, and the frequency of injections. It is crucial to follow these instructions carefully. Do not use more or less insulin or inject it more frequently than prescribed. Insulin helps control high blood sugar but does not cure diabetes. Continue using insulin even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. Do not switch brands, types, or doses of insulin without your doctor’s approval. Insulin cartridges are designed for use with dosing pens. Ensure you know the type of container your insulin comes in and the supplies you need, such as needles, syringes, or pens, to administer your medication. Verify that the name and type of insulin match your doctor’s prescription. If your insulin comes in vials, you will need syringes for injection. Be sure to use the correct syringe type (e.g., U-100 or U-500) and always use the same brand and model of needles and syringes. If you have questions about syringes, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Carefully read the manufacturer’s instructions on how to draw insulin into a syringe and inject your dose. If your insulin comes in cartridges, you may need to purchase an insulin pen separately. Follow the instructions provided with your pen and ask your doctor or pharmacist to demonstrate its use. If your insulin comes in a disposable dosing device, read the accompanying instructions carefully and ask for guidance if needed. Never reuse needles or syringes, and do not share needles, syringes, cartridges, or pens with others. If using an insulin pen, always remove the needle immediately after injecting your dose. Dispose of needles and syringes in a puncture-resistant container and consult your doctor or pharmacist on proper disposal methods. If instructed by your doctor, you may need to mix two types of insulin in the same syringe. Always draw the same type of insulin first and use the same brand of needles. Do not mix different types of insulin unless directed by your doctor. Inspect your insulin before each injection. Regular insulin (e.g., Humulin R, Novolin R) should be clear, colorless, and fluid like water. Do not use it if it appears cloudy, thickened, or discolored, or if it contains solid particles. NPH insulin (e.g., Humulin N, Novolin N) or pre-mixed insulin containing NPH (e.g., Humulin 70/30) should appear cloudy or milky after mixing. Do not use these types if clumps or solid white particles are present. Never use insulin past its expiration date. Some types of insulin require shaking or rotating to mix before use; consult your doctor or pharmacist for guidance. Your doctor or pharmacist will advise you on the appropriate injection sites, which typically include the stomach (avoiding the area within 2 inches of the belly button), upper arm, upper leg, or buttocks. Avoid injecting into muscles, scars, or moles. Rotate injection sites within the same general area (e.g., the thigh) before switching to a different area (e.g., the upper arm). Use all available sites in one area before moving to another. This medication may have other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Before using insulin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to any type of insulin or other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. Certain medications, such as alpha-blockers, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, diuretics, antidepressants, and others, may interact with insulin. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have a history of nerve damage caused by diabetes or adrenal, pituitary, thyroid, liver, or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while using insulin, contact your doctor immediately. Inform your doctor or dentist that you are using insulin if you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures. Ask your doctor for guidance on managing insulin during illness, stress, travel across time zones, or changes in exercise or activity levels, as these factors can affect your blood sugar and insulin needs. Follow all dietary and exercise recommendations provided by your doctor or dietitian. Maintain a consistent diet, eating similar amounts and types of food at the same times each day. Skipping or delaying meals or altering your food intake can disrupt blood sugar control. Alcohol may lower blood sugar levels; consult your doctor about safe alcohol consumption while using insulin. If you forget a dose, ask your doctor for specific instructions and write them down for future reference. Insulin can cause changes in blood sugar levels. Be aware of the symptoms of low (hypoglycemia) and high (hyperglycemia) blood sugar and know how to respond. Symptoms of hypoglycemia include shakiness, dizziness, sweating, irritability, mood changes, headache, numbness or tingling around the mouth, weakness, pale skin, hunger, and clumsy or jerky movements. Severe hypoglycemia can cause confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness. Ensure that family, friends, and others around you know how to respond to these symptoms and seek medical help if necessary. Symptoms of hyperglycemia include extreme thirst, frequent urination, extreme hunger, weakness, and blurred vision. Untreated hyperglycemia can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening condition with symptoms such as dry mouth, upset stomach, vomiting, shortness of breath, fruity-smelling breath, and decreased consciousness. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience these symptoms. Insulin may cause side effects, such as redness, swelling, or itching at the injection site, or changes in skin texture, fat buildup, or fat breakdown. Report severe or persistent side effects to your doctor. Serious side effects, such as rash, itching, shortness of breath, wheezing, dizziness, blurred vision, rapid heartbeat, sweating, or difficulty breathing or swallowing, require immediate medical attention. You or your doctor can report serious side effects to the FDA’s MedWatch program. Store unopened insulin vials, disposable dosing devices, and pens in the refrigerator. Do not freeze insulin or use insulin that has been frozen. Opened vials can be stored in the refrigerator or at room temperature in a cool, dry place away from heat and sunlight. Opened pens and dosing devices should be stored at room temperature. Check the manufacturer’s instructions for storage duration after first use. Dispose of expired or unused insulin properly; consult your doctor or pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual collapses or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose include those of hypoglycemia, as well as confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory for regular monitoring of blood sugar and HbA1c levels. Your doctor will also instruct you on how to monitor your blood or urine sugar levels at home. Always wear a diabetic identification bracelet to ensure proper treatment in emergencies. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist about refilling your prescription.
